div.p: The Greeks consider the Illyrians to be those peoples who dwell beyond Macedonia and Thrace, from the Chaonians and Thesprotians as far as the river Ister. This is the length of the country, while its breadth extends from the Macedonians and the mountain Thracians to the Paeonians, the Ionian Sea, and the foothills of the Alps. Its breadth is a five days' journey and its length thirty, as the Greeks also state. When the Romans measured the country, they found its length to be over six thousand stades and its width about twelve hundred.

They say that the country took its name from Illyrius, the son of Polyphemus; for the Cyclops Polyphemus and Galatea had sons, Celtus, Illyrius, and Galas, who departed from Sicily and ruled over the peoples called after them Celts, Illyrians, and Galatians. Among the many other myths told by many writers, this account pleases me best. Illyrius had sons, Encheleus, Autarieus, Dardanus, Maedus, Taulas, and Perrhaebus, and daughters, Partho, Daortho, Dassaro, and others, from whom are descended the Taulantii, Perrhaebi, Enchelees, Autarienses, Dardani, Partheni, Dassaretii, and Darsii. Autarieus himself is thought to have had a son Pannonius, or Paeon, and Paeon had sons Scordiscus and Triballus, from whom likewise the nations took their names. Let these matters be left to the antiquarians.

There are many tribes of Illyrians, as might be expected in so large a country; and still famous even today, occupying extensive territory, are the Scordisci and the Triballi, who destroyed one another in war to such an extent that whatever remnant of the Triballi survived fled across the Ister to the Getae, and a race that flourished until the time of Philip and Alexander is now extinct and its name unknown in those parts; while the Scordisci, having been reduced to extreme weakness as a result, later suffered the same fate at the hands of the Romans and fled to the islands of the same river, though in time some returned and settled on the borders of the Paeonians; hence there is even now a tribe of Scordisci among the Paeonians. In the same way the Ardiaei, who were supreme at sea, were destroyed by the Autarienses, who were supreme on land, after inflicting great damage upon them. After the Ardiaei, the Liburni became masters of the sea—another Illyrian tribe, who raided the Ionian Sea and its islands with swift, light vessels, whence the Romans even now call light, fast biremes Liburnians.

They say that the Autarienses were brought to the extremity of ruin by the wrath of Apollo. For they joined Molistomus and the Celts called Cimbri in an expedition against Delphi, and most of them perished at once before the attempt was made, when heavy rains, storms, and lightning fell upon them; and upon those who returned home came a countless multitude of frogs, which rotted and polluted the streams. Noxious vapors arose from the earth, causing a plague among the Illyrians and especially the destruction of the Autarienses, until, fleeing their own country and carrying the plague with them—since no one would receive them out of fear of it—they crossed a distance of twenty-three days' journey and settled in the marshy, uninhabited land of the Getae near the nation of the Bastarnae. As for the Celts, the god shook their land with earthquakes and overthrew their cities; nor did the calamity cease until they too, fleeing their own homes, invaded the Illyrians who had shared in their sacrilege and had been weakened by the plague, ravaged their territory, and, contracting the plague themselves, fled and plundered as far as the Pyrenees. When they turned back toward the east, the Romans, fearing from the memory of the Celts who had previously fought against them that these too might cross the Alps into Italy, marched out to meet them with their consuls and were destroyed with their whole armies. This disaster of the Romans cast a great terror of the Celts over all Italy, until the Romans chose Gaius Marius as their general—who had just waged war with distinction against the Numidians and Maurusians in Libya—and defeated the Cimbri, inflicting great slaughter upon them repeatedly, as I have related in my Gallic History. The Cimbri, now weakened and excluded from every land on account of their weakness, returned to their own country after both doing and suffering much.

Such was the end that the god imposed upon the impiety of the Illyrians and Celts. Yet they did not refrain from sacrilege, but once again, together with the Celts, the Scordisci especially among the Illyrians, along with the Maedi and Dardani, overran both Macedonia and Greece at the same time and plundered many temples, including that of Delphi, though even then they lost many men. The Romans, who were now in the thirty-second year since their first encounter with the Celts and had been at war with them at intervals ever since, made an expedition against the Illyrians on account of this sacrilege under the command of Lucius Scipio, as they were already the protectors of the Greeks and Macedonians. They say that the neighboring peoples did not join the temple-robbers as allies, but deliberately abandoned them without aid to Scipio, remembering the calamities that had fallen upon all the Illyrians because of the Autarienses. Scipio destroyed the Scordisci, and whatever remnant of them survived fled and settled on the Ister and the islands of the river; but with the Maedi and Dardani he made a treaty after accepting a bribe of the sacred gold. One of the Italian historians has remarked that it was chiefly on this account that civil wars raged more fiercely among the Romans after Lucius until the establishment of monarchy. Let this much suffice as a preface concerning those whom the Greeks consider Illyrians.

The Romans, however, distinguish both these peoples and, beyond them, the Paeonians, Rhaetians, Noricans, the Mysians in Europe, and all other neighboring peoples dwelling on the right as one sails down the Ister, from the Greeks, just as the Greeks do, and call each by its own name, yet collectively they regard them all as Illyris. How they first came to hold this view I have been unable to discover, though they still maintain it today, since they lease out the customs dues of all these nations, from the source of the Ister to the Pontic Sea, under a single contract and call it the Illyrian tax. As to how the Romans subdued them, I confessed when writing about Crete that I had not found the exact beginnings and pretexts of the wars, and I invited those able to say more to contribute to the subject; but what I myself have learned, I shall record.

Agron was king of that part of the Illyrians bordering the Ionian Gulf, which Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and his successors had formerly held. Agron in turn seized parts of Epirus, and in addition Corcyra, Epidamnus, and Pharos, and held them with garrisons. When he sailed out against the rest of the Ionian Sea as well, an island named Issa appealed to the Romans for protection. The Romans sent ambassadors with the Issaeans to learn what grievances Agron had against them. While the ambassadors were still sailing thither, Illyrian lembi put out against them and killed Cleemporus, the ambassador of the Issaeans, and Coruncanius, the Roman ambassador; the rest escaped them. Thereupon the Romans marched against the Illyrians by both sea and land. Agron died, leaving an infant son named Pinnes, and entrusted the government to his wife to act as regent for the child, although she was not the child's mother. Demetrius, who governed Pharos for Agron—for he ruled both Pharos itself and Corcyra besides—betrayed and surrendered both to the Romans as they sailed up. Next, the Romans brought Epidamnus into friendship with them and sailed to the relief of the Issaeans and Epidamnians, who were being besieged by the Illyrians. The Illyrians raised the sieges and withdrew, and some of them, called the Atintani, went over to the Romans. After this, Agron's wife sent ambassadors to Rome to restore the captives and hand over the deserters, begging pardon for what had happened not under her rule but under Agron's. The Romans replied that Corcyra, Pharos, Issa, Epidamnus, and the Atintani among the Illyrians were already Roman subjects, while Pinnes might retain the rest of Agron's kingdom and be a friend of the Romans, provided he kept away from the aforementioned places and no more than two Illyrian lembi, and those unarmed, sailed past Lissus.

She accepted all these terms, and this was the first encounter and treaty of the Romans with the Illyrians. Following this, the Romans left Corcyra and Apollonia free, and gave Demetrius certain districts as the reward of his treachery, adding that they granted them only for the time being, as they already suspected the man's faithlessness. Indeed, it soon got the better of him; for while the Romans were engaged for three years in war with the Celts around the Po, Demetrius, thinking them preoccupied, took to piracy on the sea, enlisted the Istri, another Illyrian tribe, in this enterprise, and detached the Atintani from the Romans. Once the Gallic war was settled, the Romans immediately sailed out and captured the pirates, and in the following year marched against Demetrius and the Illyrians who had joined in his offenses. Demetrius fled to Philip, king of the Macedonians, and when he returned and resumed his piracy in the Ionian Sea, they killed him and razed his native Pharos to the ground for sharing in his guilt; but they spared the Illyrians on account of Pinnes, who again sued for peace. Thus came about their second encounter and treaty with the Illyrians.
The rest of what I have found has not been written down strictly in chronological order, but rather according to each Illyrian nation.

The Romans were at war with the Macedonians, and Perseus was now king of the Macedonians after Philip. Genthius, king of another group of Illyrians, allied himself with Perseus for pay, invaded the Roman Illyrians, and threw into chains the Roman ambassadors who came to him, charging that they had come not as ambassadors but as spies. Anicius, a Roman general, sailed out and captured some of Genthius's lembi, then engaged him on land, won the battle, and shut him up in a fortress. When Genthius sued for terms from there, Anicius ordered him to surrender himself to the Romans; he asked for three days to deliberate, and was granted them. During these days, as his subjects were going over to Anicius, he asked for an interview with Anicius and fell on his knees before him in a most disgraceful manner. Anicius encouraged him in his terror, raised him up, and invited him to a banquet; but as he was leaving the dinner, he ordered his attendants to throw him into prison. Anicius led him with his children in triumph to Rome, and the entire war with Genthius was finished in twenty days. As for his seventy cities, Aemilius Paullus, the conqueror of Perseus, acting under secret instructions from the Senate, intentionally passed by them on his way to Rome and promised the terrified inhabitants that he would pardon what had happened if they brought in all the silver and gold they possessed. When they agreed, he sent a detachment of his army with them into each city, fixing the same day for all the commanders of the detachments and instructing each to proclaim at dawn in every city that they should bring their money into the marketplace within three hours, and once they had brought it together, to plunder the rest.

Thus Paullus plundered seventy cities in a single hour. The Ardaei and Palarii, other Illyrian tribes, were ravaging Roman Illyris, and the Romans, being otherwise occupied, sent ambassadors to rebuke them. When they did not mend their ways, the Romans marched against them with ten thousand infantry and six hundred cavalry. Learning of this while still unprepared, they sent ambassadors repenting and begging for peace. The Senate ordered them to make restitution for the damages to those they had wronged. When they failed to do so, Fulvius Flaccus marched against them. The war appears to have ended with a mere raid, for I have found no exact account of its conclusion. Against the Iapodes on the near side of the Alps, Sempronius, surnamed Tuditanus, and Tiberius Pandusa waged war, and the Iapodes appear to have submitted to them, as the Segestani also appear to have submitted to Lucius Cotta and Metellus; yet both peoples seem to have revolted not long afterward.

The Dalmatians, another Illyrian tribe, raided the Illyrians subject to Rome and refused to admit the Roman ambassadors who came concerning this. The Romans therefore marched against them under the consul Marcius Figulus as commander of the war. Just as Figulus was pitching camp, they sallied out, defeated his outposts, and drove him headlong from the camp down a sloping plain until he reached the river Naro in his retreat. When they withdrew and winter was beginning, Figulus, hoping to fall upon them unexpectedly, found them gathered together from their cities to meet his advance. Nevertheless, he drove them into the city of Delminium—whence indeed their name was changed to Delmateis and then to Dalmatians. Unable to accomplish anything by assault against so strong a city, and unable to use siege engines because of its height, he attacked and captured the other cities, which had been left more sparsely manned because of the concentration of troops at Delminium. Then, wrapping two-cubit clubs in pitch, sulfur, and tow, he hurled them into Delminium from catapults. Ignited by the force of their flight, they flew like torches and set fire to whatever they struck, until a great part of the city was burned down; and this was the end of Figulus's war against the Dalmatians at that time. Some time later, Caecilius Metellus, when consul, got a war voted against the Dalmatians although they had done no wrong, out of a desire for a triumph; and when they received him as a friend, he wintered among them in the city of Salona, returned to Rome, and celebrated a triumph.

When Caesar was governing Gaul, these Dalmatians and other Illyrians who were then especially prosperous seized the city of Promona from the Liburni, another Illyrian nation. The Liburni, placing themselves under Roman protection, appealed to Caesar, who was nearby. He sent word and commanded those holding Promona to restore it to the Liburni; when they paid no heed, he sent a large detachment of his army, all of whom the Illyrians killed. Caesar did not pursue the matter, for he had no leisure at that time, being embroiled in civil strife with Pompey. When the strife broke out into war, Caesar crossed the Ionian Sea from Brundisium in winter with such troops as he had and fought Pompey in Macedonia; of the rest of his army, Antony led one part to Caesar in Macedonia, likewise crossing the Ionian Sea in the depth of winter, while Gabinius led fifteen cohorts of infantry and three thousand cavalry to him through Illyris, marching around the Ionian Gulf. The Illyrians, out of fear of what they had recently done to Caesar and thinking that his victory would mean their own destruction, fell upon the entire army under Gabinius and killed them all, except Gabinius himself and a few who escaped. From such immense spoils they rose at that time to the height of wealth and power.

Caesar was necessarily occupied with Pompey, and after Pompey's downfall with the scattered remnants of his faction; once he had settled everything, he returned to Rome and prepared an expedition against the Getae and the Parthians. The Illyrians, fearing that he would attack them since they lay on his route, sent ambassadors to Rome to ask pardon for what had happened and to offer themselves in friendship and alliance, boasting of themselves as a most valiant nation. Caesar, though hastening against the Parthians, replied to them with even greater haughtiness that he would not make friends of men who had committed such deeds, but would pardon them if they submitted to tribute and gave hostages. When they promised both, he sent Vatinius with three legions and a large force of cavalry to impose a light tribute upon them and receive the hostages. Upon Caesar's assassination, however, thinking that Roman power had resided in Caesar and had perished with him, they no longer obeyed Vatinius in regard to tribute or anything else; and when he attempted to use force, they attacked and destroyed five cohorts together with their commander Baebius, a man of senatorial rank. Vatinius withdrew with the survivors to Epidamnus, and the Roman Senate entrusted this army, together with Macedonia and as much of Illyris as they controlled, to Brutus Caepio, the murderer of Gaius Caesar, at the same time as they gave Syria to Cassius, who was also one of Gaius's assassins. Yet these men too, being attacked by Antony and the second Caesar who was called Augustus, had no leisure at all to attend to the Illyrians.

The Paeonians are a great nation along the Ister, stretching lengthwise from the Iapodes to the Dardani; they are called Paeonians by the Greeks and Pannonians in Latin, and are counted by the Romans as part of Illyris, as I said before. Therefore it seems fitting to me to speak of them now in my Illyrian history. They have been famous since Macedonian times on account of the Agrianes, who rendered the greatest services to Philip and Alexander and are Paeonians of the lower Paeonians, neighbors to the Illyrians. When Cornelius marched against the Paeonians, he fared so badly that he inspired a great terror of the Paeonians in all Italians, and for a long time made subsequent consuls reluctant to campaign against the Paeonians. This is all that I was able to find concerning the earlier history of the Illyrians and Paeonians; nor in the memoirs of the second Caesar, called Augustus, did I find anything earlier about the Paeonians either.

It appears to me that besides the nations already mentioned, still other Illyrians had previously submitted to the Romans. How they did so I have not learned, for Augustus wrote not of the deeds of others but of his own: how he brought back to tribute those who had revolted, subdued others who had been independent from the beginning, and mastered all those who inhabit the summits of the Alps—barbarous and warlike nations that plundered Italy as their neighbor. It is a marvel to me that so many great Roman armies marching through the Alps against the Celts and Iberians overlooked these nations, and that not even Gaius Caesar, a man most fortunate in war, finished them off when he was fighting the Celts and wintering in this region for ten years. Yet it seems to me that the others, hurrying toward the objectives for which they had been chosen, cared only for passage through the Alps, while Gaius was absorbed in Gallic affairs, and when Pompey's civil war overtook the Gallic campaign, he postponed the completion of this task. For it is clear that he was chosen to govern Illyris along with Gaul, though he did not govern all of it, only as much of Illyris as belonged to the Romans at that time.

Augustus, however, subdued everything completely, and in contrast to the inactivity of Antony he took credit before the Senate for having pacified Italy against stubbornly resisting nations that frequently harassed it. The Oxyaei, Pertheenatae, Bathiatae, Taulantii, Cambaei, Cinambri, Meromenni, and Pyrissaei he subdued in a single campaign; with greater effort the Docleatae, Carni, Interfrurini, Naresii, Glintidiones, and Taurisci were taken and forced to pay the tributes they had defaulted on. Upon their capture, their neighbors, the Hippasini and Bessi, were struck with terror and surrendered to him. Others of them who had revolted—the Meliteni and Corcyreni, who inhabited islands—he utterly uprooted because they practiced piracy on the sea; the men of military age he put to death, and the rest he sold into slavery. From the Liburni he took away their ships, because they too practiced piracy. Among the Iapodes on the near side of the Alps, the Moentini and Avendeatae surrendered to him as he approached; the Arupini, who are the most numerous and warlike of these Iapodes, moved from their villages into their town, and as he approached fled into the woods. Caesar took the town but did not burn it, hoping they would submit; and when they submitted, he allowed them to dwell in it.

Those who gave him the most trouble were the Salassi, the Iapodes beyond the Alps, the Segestani, the Dalmatians, the Daesitiatae, and the Paeonians, who live far from the Salassi. The Salassi inhabit the summits of the Alps—rugged mountains with a narrow and difficult pass leading up to them; on this account they were independent and demanded tolls from passersby. Vetus fell upon them unexpectedly, seized the passes by ambush, and besieged them for two years. Driven by want of salt, of which they stand in particular need, they admitted garrisons. As soon as Vetus withdrew, however, they expelled the garrisons, fortified the passes, and mocked the troops sent against them by Caesar, who could accomplish nothing of importance. Hence Caesar, as the war against Antony was impending, agreed to leave them independent and unpunished for what they had done in the time of Vetus. Suspicious of this agreement, they stockpiled large quantities of salt and raided Roman territory, until Messala Corvinus was sent against them and reduced them by famine.

Thus the Salassi were subdued. As for the Iapodes beyond the Alps, a strong and fierce nation, they had twice repulsed the Romans within about twenty years, had overrun Aquileia, and had plundered Tergeste, a Roman colony. When Caesar marched against them along a steep and rugged road, they made it still more difficult for him by felling trees. When he reached the top, they fled into the rest of the forest and lay in ambush as he advanced. Caesar, who always suspected something of the sort, sent detachments to the ridges, which moved along parallel to him on either side as he advanced through the lower ground cutting down the forest. The Iapodes darted out from their ambushes and wounded many, but most of them were cut down by the troops charging down from the heights. The rest fled once more into the thickets, abandoning their city named Terponus. Caesar captured it but did not burn it, hoping that these too would submit; and submit they did.

He next marched against another city, Metulum, which is the capital of the Iapodes; it lies on a heavily wooded mountain upon two hills divided by a narrow ravine. Its youth numbered about three thousand warlike and very well-armed men, who easily repulsed the Romans when they surrounded their walls. The Romans raised an embankment, which the Metulians harassed by sallies night and day, while wearing down the men from the wall with siege engines they had obtained from the war that Decimus Brutus had fought there against Antony and Augustus. When their own wall began to give way, they built another wall inside, abandoned the damaged one, and withdrew into the newly built one. The Romans took and burned the abandoned wall, raised two embankments against the other, and from them extended four bridges to the wall. When these were ready, Caesar sent a detachment around to the rear of the city to distract the Metulians, and ordered the rest to cross over to the walls by the bridges, while he himself climbed a high tower to watch.

The barbarians met those crossing head-on along the wall, while others lying in wait below thrust at the bridges with long spears, growing bolder as one bridge and then a second collapsed. When the third also fell, complete panic seized the Romans, and no one would step onto the fourth until Caesar leaped down from the tower and upbraided them. When even this failed to rouse them, he seized a shield himself and ran onto the bridge. Alongside him ran Agrippa and Hiero among the officers, his bodyguard Lutus, and Volas—these four alone, and a few shield-bearers. As he was already crossing the bridge, the army, overcome with shame, rushed onto it in a mass. Once again the bridge collapsed under the weight, and the men were buried in a heap beneath it; some died, while others were carried off crushed. Caesar was wounded in the right leg and both arms, yet he immediately ran back up to the tower with his insignia and showed himself safe and sound, lest any panic should arise from a rumor of his death. And so that the enemy might not think he would give up and retreat, he immediately began building other bridges—a thing that terrified the Metulians most of all, seeing that they were fighting against an unconquerable will.

On the following day they sent envoys to him, gave fifty hostages whom Caesar selected, and promised to receive a garrison, yielding the higher hill to the garrison while they themselves moved over to the other. When the garrison entered and ordered them to lay down their arms, they were filled with indignation; shutting their wives and children in the council house and setting a guard over them with orders to set fire to the council house if anything untoward happened to them, they attacked the Romans in desperation. Attacking men on higher ground from below, they were overwhelmed to a man; the guards set fire to the council house, and many of the women killed themselves and their children, while others leaped into the fire carrying their children still alive, so that all the youth of the Metulians perished in the battle and most of the non-combatants in the flames. The city itself was burned along with them, and not a trace remained of what had been a very great city there. After the capture of Metulum, the rest of the Iapodes were terrified and surrendered themselves to Caesar. Thus the Iapodes beyond the Alps submitted to the Romans for the first time; and when the Poseni among them revolted after Caesar's departure, Marcus Helvius was sent against them, captured them, put the guilty to death, and sold the rest into slavery.

Into the territory of the Segestani the Romans had invaded twice before without obtaining either a hostage or anything else, which made the Segestani proud. Caesar advanced against them through the country of the Paeonians, which was not yet subject to Rome either. The country of the Paeonians is wooded and stretches lengthwise from the Iapodes to the Dardani. These Paeonians did not live in cities, but in farms or villages grouped by kinship; nor did they meet in common councils, nor did they have magistrates over all of them. Those of military age numbered up to a hundred thousand, yet even these did not assemble in a body because of their lack of central government. As Caesar approached them, they fled into the woods and killed any soldiers who strayed from the ranks. So long as Caesar hoped they would come to terms with him, he spared their villages and farms; when they did not come to meet him, he burned and ravaged everything for eight days until he reached the territory of the Segestani—who are also Paeonians—on the river Save. There stands a strong city, enclosed by the river and a very large moat, which Caesar particularly wanted to use as a supply depot for the war against the Dacians and Bastarnae, who live beyond the Ister—called here the Danube, though a little further down it becomes the Ister. The Save flows into the Ister, and Caesar had ships built on the Save to carry provisions for him into the Danube.

For these reasons Caesar needed Segesta. As he approached, the Segestani sent envoys to ask what he wanted. He replied that he wished to introduce a garrison and take a hundred hostages so that he might safely use the city as a depot against the Dacians; he also demanded as much grain as they could supply. The leading men were willing to grant these demands, but the common people grew furious: they allowed the hostages to be given, perhaps because they were not their own children but those of the leading men, yet when the garrison approached they could not bear the sight of it, and in a mad impulse they shut the gates again and manned the walls. Caesar therefore bridged the river, constructed palisades and trenches on every side, and after walling them in, raised two embankments. The Segestani made frequent sallies against these, and when they could not capture them, threw down torches and quantities of fire from above. When a relieving force of other Paeonians approached them, Caesar went out to meet it and ambushed it; some were killed, others fled, and no more Paeonians came to their aid.

The Segestani endured every hardship of the siege and were taken by storm on the thirtieth day, and only then did they begin to beg for mercy. Caesar, out of admiration for their bravery and pity for their supplication, neither killed nor uprooted them, but imposed a fine in money, walled off a part of the city, and introduced into it a garrison of twenty-five cohorts. Having accomplished this, he set out for Rome, intending to return to Illyris in the spring. When a rumor spread that the Segestani had destroyed the garrison, he hurried back in winter. He found the outcome of the rumor false, though its cause was true: the garrison had indeed been in danger when the Segestani suddenly surrounded them, and the surprise attack had cost many lives, but on the following day they had sallied forth and overpowered the Segestani. Caesar therefore marched against the Dalmatians, another Illyrian tribe bordering on the Taulantii.

Ever since the Dalmatians had destroyed the five cohorts under Gabinius and captured their standards, they had been elated by this exploit and had not laid down their arms for ten years; and now, as Caesar advanced against them, they agreed to ally with one another. Their finest fighting men numbered more than twelve thousand, and they chose Versus as their general. He again occupied Promona, the city of the Liburni, and fortified it, though it was already naturally very strong; for the place is mountainous and surrounded on all sides by hills sharp as sawteeth. The main force was in the city, while Versus placed garrisons on the hills, and all of them looked down upon the Romans from above. Caesar openly began to wall them all in, while secretly sending his boldest men to search for a way up to the highest of the hills. Under cover of the forest, they fell upon the sleeping guards by night, killed them, and signaled to Caesar in the twilight. He immediately assaulted the city with the greater part of his army, and sent detachment after detachment to the captured peak, from which they descended upon the other hills. Fear and confusion fell upon the barbarians as they were all attacked from every side at once; especially those on the hills feared being cut off from the passes because of the lack of water, and they fled together into Promona.

Caesar enclosed both the city and two hills that were still held by the enemy within a single line of circumvallation forty stades in perimeter. Meanwhile, when Testimus, a Dalmatian, brought another army to relieve those in Promona, Caesar met him and drove him into the mountains; and while Testimus was still looking on, he captured Promona before the circumvallation was even completed. For when the besieged made a sally and were swiftly driven back, the Romans burst into the city along with the fugitives and killed a third of them inside; the rest fled up to the citadel, where a Roman cohort guarded them at the gates. On the fourth night the barbarians fell upon them, and the cohort abandoned the gates in terror. Caesar checked the enemy's charge and on the next day received their surrender; as for the cohort that had abandoned its post, he drew lots and punished every tenth man with death, along with two centurions in addition to the tenth, and ordered that for the rest of that summer the survivors be given barley instead of wheat for their rations.

Thus Promona was taken. Seeing this, Testimus dispersed his army, bidding them flee in different directions, so that the Romans could not pursue them far, fearing to divide themselves into many detachments, unfamiliar with the roads, and baffled by the confused tracks of flight. They captured Synodium, a city at the edge of the forest where the Dalmatians had ambushed Gabinius's army in a deep, long ravine between two mountains—where they were also laying an ambush for Caesar. Caesar burned Synodium, sent troops along the mountain heights on both sides to escort him, and marched himself through the ravine, felling the forest, capturing the towns, and burning everything he took along the way. While he was besieging the city of Setovia, a relieving force of barbarians approached, which Caesar met and prevented from rushing into Setovia. In this engagement he was struck on the knee by a stone and was laid up for many days. Upon recovering, he returned to Rome to enter upon his consulship with Volcatius Tullus, leaving Statilius Taurus to finish the remainder of the war.

Having entered upon his consulship on the first day of the year and resigned the office on the very same day to Autronius Paetus, he immediately hurried back against the Dalmatians, still holding the office of the triumvirate—for two years still remained of the second five-year term of this office, which the triumvirs had voted to themselves after the first and which the people had ratified. The Dalmatians, already worn down by famine because they were cut off from outside markets, came out to meet Caesar as he approached and surrendered themselves as suppliants, giving seven hundred children as hostages, as Caesar demanded, together with the Roman standards of Gabinius; and pledging to pay the tribute that had been in arrears since Gaius Caesar's time, they remained obedient thereafter. Caesar deposited the standards in the portico called the Portico of Octavia. After the capture of the Dalmatians, the Derbani also met Caesar as he approached, begged pardon as suppliants, gave hostages, and pledged to pay their overdue tributes. As for the those whom Caesar approached gave hostages as well on the terms of their treaties; those whom he did not approach on account of illness neither gave hostages nor made treaties, though these too appear to have been subdued later.

Thus Caesar mastered the whole land of Illyris, both the part that had revolted from Rome and that which had never previously submitted to them. The Senate voted him an Illyrian triumph, which he celebrated later together with his triumphs over Antony.

There remain of what the Romans consider Illyris the Rhaetians and Noricans before the Paeonians, and after the Paeonians the Mysians as far as the Euxine Sea. The Rhaetians and Noricans I suppose were subdued either by Gaius Caesar when he was fighting the Celts, or by Augustus when he was conquering the Paeonians; for they lie between the two, and I have found no separate account of anything done against the Rhaetians or Noricans, whence it seems to me that they were conquered along with one or the other of their neighbors.

As for the Mysians, Marcus Lucullus, the brother of Licinius Lucullus who fought against Mithridates, overran them and advanced to the river, where there are six Greek cities bordering on the Mysians—Istrus, Dionysopolis, Odessus, Mesembria, Callatis, and Apollonia, from which he carried off to Rome the great statue of Apollo dedicated on the Palatine. I have found nothing further done against the Mysians under the Roman Republic, nor were they reduced to tribute even under Augustus; they were subdued by Tiberius, who became emperor of the Romans after Augustus. However, all events prior to the capture of Egypt that occurred under the authority of the people have been written by me separately, whereas what these emperors conquered or annexed after Egypt has been related as their own deeds after the history of the Republic; and there I shall speak more fully about the Mysians. For the present, since the Romans consider the Mysians part of Illyris and this book of mine is the Illyrian History, to make the work complete it seemed right to state in advance that the Mysians too were overrun by Lucullus as general of the people and subdued by Tiberius under imperial power.
